title: ResNet
one_sentence_summary: Residual Networks use identity shortcuts to make very deep networks easier to optimize.
quick_recall: A residual block learns a change F(x), then adds the original input: y = F(x) + x. The shortcut gives information and gradients a direct route through the network.
core_explanation: Simply stacking layers can produce higher training error as depth grows—not because the model lacks capacity, but because optimization becomes difficult. ResNet reframes a block as learning a residual function F(x) relative to its input. If no transformation is useful, driving F(x) toward zero is easier than forcing several nonlinear layers to reproduce an identity mapping. The addition also creates short paths through the network, improving signal propagation.
why_it_matters: ResNet made reliably training networks with dozens or hundreds of layers practical and established skip connections as a standard design pattern.
historical_context: He et al. introduced ResNet in 2015; the approach won the ILSVRC 2015 classification task and influenced architectures far beyond vision.

architecture.description: The main branch applies convolution, normalization and activation. The identity branch bypasses those transformations, and both branches are added before the output activation.

how_to_read: Follow x through the learned transformation F(x).
Notice the separate identity path that carries x unchanged.
The two paths meet at addition, producing F(x) + x.
The block only needs to learn the useful change relative to x.

limitations: More depth still increases compute and memory
The simplest identity shortcut requires matching tensor dimensions
